title: The ancient God hidden in the cave
theme: Death begins his answer: the wise one who knows, by inward yoga, the God hard to see — hidden, entered deep within, set in the cave, dwelling in the depths, ancient — leaves joy and sorrow behind.

words.context: Śaṅkara: because it is very subtle, «अतिसूक्ष्मत्वात्»

words.meaning: by the attainment of inward yoga

sandhi.rule: A final m becomes anusvāra before a consonant, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः); so throughout the first line.
Like vowels join long, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).
The visarga after a becomes u before h, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च), and a + u give o, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः).

samasa.meaning: whose seeing is hard: hard to see
standing in the depth; the locative ending is kept
the attainment of inward yoga (adhyātma, ‘concerning the self’, is itself an avyayībhāva)

morphology.note: The locative gahvare is kept inside the compound, and the s of √sthā becomes ṣ after e.
Past participle of anu-pra-√viś, ‘entered after, entered into’: for Śaṅkara, covered by the knowledge of objects; for Raṅgarāmānuja, entered into all beings.

translation.literal: Having known by the attainment of inward yoga that God, hard to see, hidden, entered in, set in the cave, dwelling in the depth, ancient, the wise one leaves joy and sorrow.
translation.readable: That ancient God is hard to see: hidden, entered deep within, set in the cave of the heart, dwelling in the depths. The wise one who comes to know him by turning inward leaves joy and sorrow behind.

anvaya: धीरः अध्यात्मयोगाधिगमेन तम् दुर्दर्शम् गूढम् अनुप्रविष्टम् गुहाहितम् गह्वरेष्ठम् पुराणम् देवम् मत्वा हर्षशोकौ जहाति ।
syntax: One sentence. Six accusative adjectives describe tam … devam, the object of the absolutive matvā; the instrumental adhyātmayogādhigamena gives the means; the subject dhīraḥ and the verb jahāti stand at the end.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the Self (devam = «आत्मानं»), hidden in the intellect; the wise lose joy and sorrow because the Self has neither rise nor fall — «आत्मन उत्कर्षापकर्षयोरभावात्». Raṅgarāmānuja: the supreme Self, the inner controller, known through knowledge of the individual self — «जीवात्मज्ञानस्य परमात्मज्ञानहेतुत्वादिति भावः». Madhva: the Lord, dwelling in the freed soul — «गह्वरे मुक्तजीवे स्थितम्».

Śaṅkara: standing in the depth, a rough place full of troubles — «गह्वरे विषमे अनेकानर्थसङ्कटे तिष्ठतीति गह्वरेष्ठम्»; Raṅgarāmānuja: the inner controller of the self; Madhva: the depth is the freed soul.

Śaṅkara defines it: «विषयेभ्यः प्रतिसंहृत्य चेतस आत्मनि समाधानमध्यात्मयोगः», withdrawing the mind from objects and settling it in the self. Raṅgarāmānuja uses almost the same words and points ahead to 1.3.13 and 2.3.10, where this practice is described; the ‘attainment’ he takes as knowledge of the individual self.

beginner: Here Death begins to answer the boy’s great question. He speaks of something hard to see. It is hidden, it has entered deep inside, it rests in a cave — the commentators say the heart or the intellect — and it lives in a dark and difficult place. It is also ancient, older than anything else. How is it found? By turning attention inward, away from the objects of the senses, and letting it rest in oneself. A person who comes to know it this way is called wise, and such a person lets go of both elation and grief. Śaṅkara says this is because the Self never rises or falls, so there is nothing in it to celebrate or mourn. Raṅgarāmānuja and Madhva say the God is the Lord who dwells within the self and is distinct from it. All agree that it is found within.
analogy: Like a spring beneath a house: searching the rooms will not find it; one has to go down.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: He describes the one to be known as hard to see, hidden, entered in, set in the cave, dwelling in the depth and ancient, and says that the wise one who knows this God through inward yoga leaves joy and sorrow.

commentary.q: Why is it hard to see, and how is it known?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: it is very subtle, and hidden by ordinary knowledge of objects — «प्राकृतविषयविज्ञानैः प्रच्छन्नमित्येतत्». It is in the cave, the intellect, because it is perceived there: «गुहायां बुद्धौ हितं निहितं स्थितं तत्रोपलभ्यमानत्वात्». Inward yoga is withdrawing the mind from objects and settling it in the self: «विषयेभ्यः प्रतिसंहृत्य चेतस आत्मनि समाधानमध्यात्मयोगः». The wise lose joy and sorrow because the Self neither rises nor falls: «आत्मन उत्कर्षापकर्षयोरभावात्».

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: the answer to the third question
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: With this verse and the next Death answers the third question («तं दुर्दर्शम् इत्यादिना मन्त्रद्वयेन»). The God is in the cave of the heart, «हृदयगुहावर्तिनम्», and dwells in the depth as the inner controller of the self, «आत्मान्तर्यामिणम्». The attainment by inward yoga is knowledge of the individual self, which leads to knowledge of the supreme: «जीवात्मज्ञानस्य परमात्मज्ञानहेतुत्वादिति भावः».

commentary.q: Madhva: the depth is the freed soul
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Madhva’s one comment on the verse: «गह्वरे मुक्तजीवे स्थितम्» — the Lord stands in the depth, the freed soul.

commentary.q: The God of this verse and the God of 1.1.17
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Commenting on the next verse, Raṅgarāmānuja argues that devam here cannot mean the individual self. In 1.1.17 the word stands beside marks of the soul; here there are none. He adds that the Bhāṣyakāra, under Brahmasūtra 1.2.11, takes the entry into the cave in this verse as the supreme Self’s: «परमात्मनस्तावत्» … «गुहाप्रवेशो दृश्यते इत्युक्तम्». Śaṅkara, by contrast, reads devam simply as the Self.

advaita.text: The God is the Self — «देवम् आत्मानं» — hidden in the intellect; knowing it ends joy and sorrow, because the Self has no rise or fall.

visistadvaita.text: The God is the supreme Self, the inner controller («आत्मान्तर्यामिणम्»), known through knowledge of the individual self: «जीवात्मज्ञानस्य परमात्मज्ञानहेतुत्वादिति भावः».

dvaita.text: The Lord dwells in the freed soul: «गह्वरे मुक्तजीवे स्थितम्».

schools.disagreement: Whether the God hidden in the cave is the knower’s own Self (Śaṅkara) or the Lord within the soul and distinct from it (Raṅgarāmānuja, Madhva).

parallels.note: The Brahmasūtra speaks of ‘the two selves that have entered the cave’. Raṅgarāmānuja (on 1.2.13) reports that the Bhāṣyakāra reads this verse under that sūtra.
The Kaṭha returns to the cave in 1.3.1, where two have entered it.
A few verses later the Self is again ‘set in the cave of this creature’.

contemporary.text: The verse says what is most real is hard to see because attention is occupied elsewhere — Śaṅkara says covered by the ordinary knowledge of objects. A day full of notifications illustrates the point: nothing hides an inner life so well as a steady supply of outer things to look at. The verse’s remedy is not more information but a turning back of attention. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: When did you last spend ten minutes without looking at anything outside yourself?
reflect.deeper: Why might joy and sorrow both be left behind, and not only sorrow? Is losing joy a loss?
reflect.practice: Sit quietly for five minutes and notice how often attention runs outward. Do not judge it; only notice it.

flags.note: devam: the Self (Śaṅkara), or the supreme Self within the soul and distinct from it (Raṅgarāmānuja, Madhva).
